pr.title: Fix generator and analyzer crash on closed generic struct from a referenced assembly (REQ-2283)
pr.body:
Requirement: REQ-2283

Agent-written implementation of requirement REQ-2283 (upstream MessagePack-CSharp issue 2283), from the Junction 2026 challenge branch `ju26-issue-2283`.

Author: coding agent. Accountable owner: to be assigned by Countersign.
pr.author: ToukoUrsin

requirement.title: Generator and analyzer crash with IndexOutOfRangeException on a closed generic struct from a referenced assembly
requirement.body:
#### Bug description

Both `MessagePackGenerator` (CS8785) and `MsgPack00xMessagePackAnalyzer` (AD0001) throw `IndexOutOfRangeException` when a `[MessagePackObject]` type has a member whose type is a **closed generic value type defined in a referenced assembly**.

Because the generator then "will not contribute to the output", the compiling assembly silently ends up with **no generated resolver at all**. It is only a warning, so a normal build looks fine, but trimmed and NativeAOT apps fail at runtime. In our case three assemblies of a large app had been shipping without a resolver across two releases before we noticed.

#### Repro steps

Two projects. `lib`:

```csharp
using MessagePack;
namespace Lib;

[MessagePackObject]
public partial record struct Item<T>([property: Key(0)] string Key);
```

`app`, with a `ProjectReference` to `lib`:

```csharp
using MessagePack; using Lib;
namespace App;

[MessagePackObject]
public sealed partial record Cmd([property: Key(0)] string Scope)
{
    [Key(1)] public Item<int> Member { get; init; }
}
```

Then `dotnet build` on `app`. Both projects are in the attached `mp-repro.zip`.

#### Expected behavior

A clean build, with a generated resolver in `app`.
#### Actual behavior

```
CSC : warning CS8785: Generator 'MessagePackGenerator' failed to generate source. It will not
contribute to the output and compilation errors may occur as a result. Exception was of type
'IndexOutOfRangeException' with message 'Index was outside the bounds of the array.'.
CSC : warning AD0001: Analyzer 'MessagePack.SourceGenerator.Analyzers.MsgPack00xMessagePackAnalyzer'
threw an exception of type 'System.IndexOutOfRangeException' with message 'Index was outside the
bounds of the array.'.
```

`app.dll` contains no `GeneratedMessagePackResolver`.

- Version used: MessagePack 3.1.8
- Runtime: .NET 10 (SDK 10.0.204), Windows 11

#### Additional context

**What triggers it.** `Item` is declared in `lib`, `Cmd` in `app`:

| `Item` declared as | result |
|---|---|
| `record struct Item<T>` | **crash** |
| `struct Item<T>` | **crash** |
| `struct Item` | ok |
| `record struct Item` | ok |
| `class Item<T>` | ok |
| `record class Item<T>` | ok |

So it needs all three of: **generic**, **value type**, **from a referenced assembly**. Moving the identical `Item<T>` declaration into `app` itself makes the crash disappear, which is what makes this specific to metadata symbols.
**Stack trace.**

```
System.IndexOutOfRangeException: Index was outside the bounds of the array.
   at TypeCollector.GetObjectInfo(INamedTypeSymbol formattedType, ISymbol callerSymbol)
   at TypeCollector.CollectGeneric(INamedTypeSymbol type, ISymbol callerSymbol) in TypeCollector.cs:line 661
   at TypeCollector.CollectCore(ITypeSymbol typeSymbol, ISymbol callerSymbol) in TypeCollector.cs:line 371
   at TypeCollector.GetObjectInfo(INamedTypeSymbol formattedType, ISymbol callerSymbol) in TypeCollector.cs:line 1062
   at TypeCollector.CollectCore(ITypeSymbol typeSymbol, ISymbol callerSymbol) in TypeCollector.cs:line 386
   at TypeCollector.Collect() in TypeCollector.cs:line 300
   at MsgPack00xMessagePackAnalyzer.AnalyzeSymbol(SymbolAnalysisContext, ReferenceSymbols, AnalyzerOptions) in MsgPack00xMessagePackAnalyzer.cs:line 431
```

`CollectGeneric` line 661 is the closed-generic branch that calls `GetObjectInfo` directly:

```csharp
else
{
    // NOTE: ... closed generic types such as `Foo<string>` are not registered as a formatter.
    this.GetObjectInfo(type, callerSymbol);
```

so `GetObjectInfo` runs against a type that has no syntax. Several diagnostic paths inside it index `DeclaringSyntaxReferences[0]` directly (lines 735, 1009, 1101) instead of using `FirstOrDefault()` the way the neighbouring `GetIdentifierLocation` / `GetLocation` / `GetParameterListLocation` helpers already do, and that collection is empty for a metadata symbol. I did not narrow down which of the three fires.

**Getting the stack trace.** Console output truncates the exception to its message; `-p:ErrorLog=out.sarif` preserves the full description, including the stack trace and an `ISymbol:` context line naming the offending type:

```
dotnet build -p:ErrorLog=out.sarif
```

**Workaround.** Putting `[MessagePackFormatter(typeof(ItemFormatter<>))]` on the generic value type short-circuits `CollectCore` (line 356) before `GetObjectInfo` is reached, at the cost of hand-writing the formatter.

**Possibly related:** #2092 reports CS8785 from the v3 generator, but with a different inner exception and no repro.

[mp-repro.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30408133/mp-repro.zip)

criteria.note: Theory (record struct Item<T> and struct Item<T>): builds Lib in memory, references it as a metadata image from the repro App source, runs MessagePackGenerator, and asserts the generator throws no exception and reports no CS8785.

criteria.text: In the same scenario, building the referencing project does not produce warning AD0001 for MsgPack00xMessagePackAnalyzer, and no IndexOutOfRangeException is thrown.
criteria.note: Theory (both crashing forms): runs MsgPack00xMessagePackAnalyzer through CompilationWithAnalyzers on the repro App compilation and asserts no analyzer exception (IndexOutOfRangeException included) and no AD0001 diagnostic.

criteria.text: The compiled referencing assembly in the repro (app.dll) contains a generated GeneratedMessagePackResolver.
criteria.sourceQuote: A clean build, with a generated resolver in `app`.
criteria.note: After running the generator on the repro App (record struct form), asserts that a GeneratedMessagePackResolver type exists in the output compilation, that there are no compile errors, and that Emit succeeds.

criteria.text: Both declaration forms that currently crash, `record struct Item<T>` and `struct Item<T>` declared in a referenced assembly, are covered by a regression test that builds without generator or analyzer exceptions.
criteria.sourceQuote: So it needs all three of: **generic**, **value type**, **from a referenced assembly**.
criteria.note: Supported by the PR author’s own tests (which do fail without the change), not by an independent probe.

criteria.text: Analyzer diagnostics that the analyzer would report against a closed generic metadata type are either reported without an exception or skipped; neither component crashes.
criteria.sourceQuote: Several diagnostic paths inside it index `DeclaringSyntaxReferences[0]` directly (lines 735, 1009, 1101) instead of using `FirstOrDefault()`
criteria.note: The referenced generic struct has members with no Key attribute, which would trigger MsgPack004. Asserts that neither the generator nor the analyzer throws on the closed Item<int> metadata type, and that there is no CS8785 or AD0001.

criteria.text: All existing generator and analyzer tests still pass, and diagnostics for source-declared types (including generic value types declared in the same project) are still reported at the same source locations as before.
criteria.note: With a generic struct declared in the same project and used as Item<int>, asserts that the analyzer reports exactly the same MsgPack004 diagnostics at the property identifier span (9,19-9,24) as before: two for Item<T> and one for Item<int>.

story.headline: A [MessagePackObject] type can now use a closed generic struct from a referenced assembly without crashing the generator or the analyzer, so the consuming assembly gets its generated resolver again.
story.before: When a member's type was a closed generic value type from another assembly (e.g. Lib.Item<int>), TypeCollector.GetObjectInfo indexed DeclaringSyntaxReferences[0] on metadata symbols that have no syntax. Both the generator (CS8785) and MsgPack00x analyzer (AD0001) threw IndexOutOfRangeException. The generator then produced nothing, so the app had no GeneratedMessagePackResolver and only a build warning showed it.
story.after: The diagnostic paths in GetObjectInfo get a null location when a member has no syntax, so they no longer throw. TypeCollector also drops any analyzer diagnostic whose location is not in source or is not in the compilation being analyzed. The build is clean and the resolver is generated.

steps.text: In GetObjectInfo, the BothStringAndIntKeyAreNull and MemberNeedsKey reports no longer index DeclaringSyntaxReferences[0]. They use FirstOrDefault or the new GetPropertyIdentifierLocation, which returns null for metadata members. This removes the crash.

The TypeCollector constructor now wraps the analyzer's report callback in ReportIfLocatedInCompilation. A diagnostic is passed on only if Location.IsInSource and compilation.ContainsSyntaxTree(...) are both true. Everything else is dropped without a message. The generator path passes no callback, so the wrapper does not change it.

Three tests in GenericsFormatterTests compile a defining assembly to a metadata image. A consumer then uses Item<int> as a struct, as a record struct, and as a struct with an unkeyed member. The tests assert there are no warnings and that the resolver is generated.

The README and the MsgPack004 docs now say that closed generic types from referenced assemblies are supported. They also say that diagnostics about those types' members are reported only by the assembly that defines them.

alsoTouches: Every analyzer diagnostic raised through TypeCollector now passes the in-compilation location filter. A diagnostic with a null or metadata location is dropped without a message instead of being reported.

BothStringAndIntKeyAreNull now uses the property's identifier location only when the property's syntax is a PropertyDeclarationSyntax. For other declarations, such as positional record parameters, the location is null and the filter drops the diagnostic.
Diagnostics about members of types from referenced assemblies are no longer reported in the consuming project at any severity.
The README and the MsgPack004 docs now include a statement about where diagnostics are reported for types from referenced assemblies.

diagrams.title: Metadata-safe diagnostics in TypeCollector
diagrams.caption: Both the generator and the analyzer reach GetObjectInfo through CollectGeneric. The fix is a null-safe location lookup plus a filter on every analyzer diagnostic, not only the ones that crashed.

diagrams.title: Building app with Cmd { Item<int> Member }
diagrams.caption: Before, GetObjectInfo threw while indexing empty syntax references. Now it gets a null location, the diagnostic is filtered out, and the resolver is generated.

units.title: Drop analyzer diagnostics not located in the current compilation
units.summary: TypeCollector now wraps its diagnostic callback so a diagnostic is only reported if its location is in source and belongs to the compilation being analyzed; everything else is silently dropped. This also adds the helper that finds a property's identifier location only when the property is declared in source.

hunks.header: @@ -1636,6 +1636,11 @@ Two assembly-level attributes exist to help with mixing in your own custom forma

lines.s: Learn more about using a mix of your own custom formatters and automatically generated ones in [the Analyzer section](#analyzer).

Closed generic types defined in a referenced assembly (for example, `Item<int>` where `Item<T>` is defined in another project or NuGet package) can be used as members of your `[MessagePackObject]` types, including generic value types and record structs.
Diagnostics about the members of such a type are reported by the assembly that defines it rather than by the consuming project, so any problem must be fixed there.

[MagicOnion](https://github.com/Cysharp/MagicOnion) is a code-first gRPC framework based on grpc-dotnet and MessagePack. gRPC usually communicates with Protocol Buffers using IDL. But MagicOnion uses MessagePack for C# and does not need IDL. When communicating C# to C#, schemaless (or rather C# classes as schema) is better than using IDL.
This analyzer only reports on members declared in the project being compiled.
Members of a type defined in a referenced assembly are reported by the project that defines that type, so an unattributed public member of such a type must be fixed in its defining project.

private TypeCollector(Compilation compilation, AnalyzerOptions options, ReferenceSymbols referenceSymbols, ITypeSymbol targetType, Action<Diagnostic>? reportAnalyzerDiagnostic, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
this.reportDiagnostic = reportAnalyzerDiagnostic is null ? null : diagnostic => ReportIfLocatedInCompilation(reportAnalyzerDiagnostic, diagnostic);
var stringKey = key is { Value: string stringKeyValue } ? stringKeyValue : default;

/// Reports a diagnostic only when its location belongs to the compilation being analyzed.
/// Types and members that come from metadata (or from another compilation) have no location in the compilation being analyzed.
/// Their problems are reported by the compilation that defines them, so they are dropped here rather than being reported

evidence.conclusion: A skeptic agent wrote a test asserting the correct behaviour; Countersign ran it on the PR head and it fails (2 failing). I wrote CountersignFinding1. It builds a library with `[MessagePackObject] Wrapper<T> { [Key(0)] T Content }` in both class and struct form and emits it as a metadata-only image. It then runs MsgPack00xMessagePackAnalyzer on an app where `[MessagePackObject] Cmd` has a member of type `Wrapper<Foo>` and `Foo` has no attribute. Both cases fail with an empty diagnostic list: no MsgPack003 and no AD0001. So the problem with Foo is silently lost. The cause is that MsgPack003 is placed at the metadata property `Wrapper<Foo>.Content` (callerSymbol.Locations[0]), and the new ReportIfLocatedInCompilation filter drops any diagnostic not located in the current compilation's source. Foo is then already in alreadyCollected, so it is never reported against the source member. The PR introduced this: base passed reportAnalyzerDiagnostic through unfiltered, and Roslyn only rejects source locations outside the compilation, not metadata locations. By reading, the base class case therefore reported MsgPack003 at the metadata location without crashing, because Key(0) is present and the indexing paths at lines 982 and 1074 are not reached. I could not run the base, because the tool has no base worktree.

evidence.title: Cross-checked: New docs promise diagnostics from the defining assembly that
evidence.conclusion: The cited code exists verbatim in the PR head, and a second agent instructed to refute the finding could not. The finding holds. In TypeCollector.ReportIfLocatedInCompilation (TypeCollector.cs:1444-1450), the consuming compilation silently throws away any diagnostic whose location is not a source tree in the current compilation. Nothing checks that the defining assembly ran the analyzer or kept MsgPack004 enabled. Even so, README.md:1642 and MsgPack004.md:51-52 say without qualification that these problems "are reported by" the defining project. If the package was built without the analyzer or with NoWarn, no diagnostic appears anywhere, which contradicts the documented promise. The new sections describe the new filtering behaviour, so they appear to come from this PR. I couldn't diff against base to prove it, and I didn't check whether the requirement really leaves this as an open question.

refs.quote: Diagnostics about the members of such a type are reported by the assembly that defines it rather than by the consuming project, so any problem must be fixed there.
This analyzer only reports on members declared in the project being compiled.

findings.title: MsgPack003 silently lost when an unattributed local type is used through a referenced generic
findings.body: The new filter drops every diagnostic whose location is not in a syntax tree of the current compilation. `TypeMustBeMessagePackObject` is located at `callerSymbol.Locations[0]`, and when a type is reached through a member of a referenced generic (e.g. `Wrapper<T>.Content`), the caller symbol is that metadata property, so the diagnostic is now discarded. The later visit of the type argument with the source member as caller returns early because the type is already in `alreadyCollected`, so nothing is reported. The defining assembly cannot report it either, since there `T` is a type parameter; this contradicts the new README sentence. This also changes behaviour for referenced generic classes, which did not crash before. I traced this by reading the code only; nothing was executed.
findings.scenario: lib: `[MessagePackObject] public class Wrapper<T> { [Key(0)] public T Content { get; set; } }` (or the struct form). app: `public class Foo { }` (no attribute) and `[MessagePackObject] public class Cmd { [Key(0)] public Wrapper<Foo> Value { get; set; } }`. The analyzer reaches Foo with callerSymbol = `Wrapper<Foo>.Content` (metadata location), and the MsgPack003 diagnostic is dropped. App builds with no diagnostic and the resolver has no formatter for Foo.

refs.quote: Location location = callerSymbol is not null ? callerSymbol.Locations[0] : formattedType.Locations[0];
Diagnostics about the members of such a type are reported by the assembly that defines it rather than by the consuming project, so any problem must be fixed there.

findings.suggestion: When recursing into members of a type that is not declared in this compilation, keep the nearest in-compilation caller symbol (the app member such as `Cmd.Value`) for locating diagnostics, instead of replacing it with the metadata member. Alternatively, in the filter, relocate rather than drop diagnostics about types that are declared in this compilation. Add a test with a referenced `Wrapper<T>` and an unattributed local type argument that expects MsgPack003 on the app member.

findings.title: BothStringAndIntKeyAreNull is now silently dropped for source positional record properties
findings.body: `GetPropertyIdentifierLocation` only recognises `PropertyDeclarationSyntax`. A positional record property is declared by a `ParameterSyntax`, so the helper returns null, the diagnostic gets `Location.None`, and the new filter discards it. The member is then skipped by the `else if (stringKey is not null)` branch and silently left out of serialization. The sibling MemberNeedsKey path at lines 925-926 already handles `ParameterSyntax`. Before this change the hard cast would have thrown here, so this turns a crash into a silent drop rather than a correct report.
findings.scenario: Source in the compiling project: `[MessagePackObject] public record R([property: Key(null)] string A);`. The key is neither int nor string, location is null, the diagnostic is filtered out, and `A` is omitted from the formatter with no warning.
findings.suggestion: Handle `ParameterSyntax` in the helper as line 926 does, or fall back to the syntax node's own location. More generally, the filter should not discard a `Location.None` diagnostic about a symbol that is declared in the current compilation.

findings.title: New docs promise diagnostics from the defining assembly that the code cannot guarantee
findings.body: The README and MsgPack004.md state as fact that problems in a referenced-assembly type "are reported by the assembly that defines it". That is only true if the defining project runs the MessagePack analyzer with those rules enabled; nothing in this change checks that. The requirement did not ask for a documented policy and lists this behaviour as an open question. The docs therefore commit the project to a user-visible contract that nobody has decided on.
findings.scenario: A NuGet package built without the analyzer (or with MsgPack004 as NoWarn) ships a generic struct with an unkeyed public member. The consumer reads the README, expects the defect to have been reported upstream, and gets no diagnostic anywhere.

refs.quote: Diagnostics about the members of such a type are reported by the assembly that defines it rather than by the consuming project, so any problem must be fixed there.
This analyzer only reports on members declared in the project being compiled.

findings.suggestion: Hold the doc change until the diagnostic policy is decided, or reword it to say that the consuming project does not report these and that the defining project reports them only if it runs the analyzer.

refusals.question: When a rule is broken by a type or member that lives in a referenced assembly, should the consuming project's analyzer drop the diagnostic, report it without a location, or report it on the consuming member that uses the type?
refusals.why: The requirement leaves this open. It is a product decision about what users see, and this PR picks one answer (drop) and documents it as policy in the README and MsgPack004.md.

options.label: Drop (as implemented)
options.consequence: No crash and no noise in the consumer. Problems in a library built without this analyzer (or with it disabled) are never surfaced, and problems caused by the consumer's own type arguments are lost, as in the first finding.

options.label: Report on the consuming member
options.consequence: The consumer sees an actionable location such as `Cmd.Member`. It needs caller-symbol plumbing in TypeCollector and may show errors the consumer cannot fix for third-party packages.

options.label: Report with no location
options.consequence: Nothing is lost, but the diagnostics have no file or line and may fail builds on issues in external packages.

refusals.context: The filter applies to every diagnostic routed through TypeCollector in the analyzer path, not only the three sites named in the issue. The docs added by this PR state that the defining assembly reports such problems; that holds only if that assembly ran this analyzer. The UnkeyedMember test asserts the drop behaviour.

This analyzer only reports on members declared in the project being compiled.

canaries.description: Skips the compilation-location filter, so diagnostics for members declared in metadata or another compilation get reported with no location or a location outside this compilation, which analyzers are not allowed to do.  `this.reportDiagnostic = reportAnalyzerDiagnostic is null ? null : diagnostic => ReportIfLocatedInCompilation(r` → `this.reportDiagnostic = reportAnalyzerDiagnostic;`
canaries.note: Reviewer: “ReportIfLocatedInCompilation is never called; metadata-type diagnostics are still reported”

canaries.description: Swaps the message format arguments, so the BothStringAndIntKeyAreNull message puts the property name where the type name belongs and the type name where the property name belongs.  `this.reportDiagnostic?.Invoke(Diagnostic.Create(MsgPack00xMessagePackAnalyzer.BothStringAndIntKeyAreNull, GetP` → `this.reportDiagnostic?.Invoke(Diagnostic.Create(MsgPack00xMessagePackAnalyzer.BothStringAndIntKeyAreNull, GetP`
canaries.note: Reviewer: “BothStringAndIntKeyAreNull message arguments were swapped (member name now precedes type)”

canaries.description: Uses the type's name instead of the field's name in the MemberNeedsKey message, so the diagnostic no longer says which field is missing a key.  `: Diagnostic.Create(MsgPack00xMessagePackAnalyzer.MemberNeedsKey, item.DeclaringSyntaxReferences.FirstOrDefaul` → `: Diagnostic.Create(MsgPack00xMessagePackAnalyzer.MemberNeedsKey, item.DeclaringSyntaxReferences.FirstOrDefaul`
canaries.note: Reviewer: “MsgPack004 for unkeyed fields now prints the type name instead of the field name”

canaries.description: Returns the location of the whole property declaration instead of just its identifier, so the diagnostic covers the wrong span and tests or code fixes that expect the identifier position break.  `private static Location? GetPropertyIdentifierLocation(IPropertySymbol property) => (property.DeclaringSyntaxR` → `private static Location? GetPropertyIdentifierLocation(IPropertySymbol property) => (property.DeclaringSyntaxR`
canaries.note: Reviewer: “MsgPack005 on properties now spans the whole declaration instead of the identifier”
